props.title: The American Soldier
props.initialSlug: A cold-blooded hitman returns to Munich for revenge

sections.content: **The American Soldier (1970)** (1970) stands as one of Rainer Werner Fassbinder's most provocative early works, merging film noir conventions with his signature New German Cinema style. The film follows Ricky, a Vietnam vet turned hitman, prefiguring later examinations of veteran alienation like **Taxi Driver** (1976) and **Rolling Thunder** (1977). Fassbinder's stark black-and-white cinematography and deliberately artificial staging create a Brechtian distance that forces viewers to critically examine post-war German society and American cultural imperialism.

sections.content: Fassbinder's treatment of violence and masculinity in **The American Soldier** (1970) directly influenced later European crime films like Jean-Pierre Melville's **Un Flic** (1972) and influenced American neo-noir. The film's detached style and focus on a returning soldier's alienation created a template for examining post-Vietnam trauma that would be expanded in films like **Coming Home** (1978) and **The Deer Hunter** (1978).

The film's examination of American cultural influence on post-war Germany connects to broader New German Cinema movements, alongside works like Wim Wenders' **Kings of the Road** (1976) and Werner Herzog's **Stroszek** (1977). Fassbinder's use of genre conventions while simultaneously subverting them became a hallmark of his style, reaching its apex in later works like **The Marriage of Maria Braun** (1979). sections.content: **The American Soldier** (1970) marked a crucial moment in New German Cinema's engagement with American genres. While contemporaries like Volker Schlöndorff with **The Lost Honor of Katharina Blum** (1975) took more straightforward approaches to genre, Fassbinder's deconstructive style influenced later German filmmakers like Christian Petzold, whose **Phoenix** (2014) and **Transit** (2018) continue this tradition of genre reinvention.
